INTRODUCTION 

Understanding the difference between commercial real estate and residential real estate investing is as simple as knowing the difference between a home that people live in and a business that people work in. When figuring out how to make money with commercial real estate, you need to find out what will be popular in your area. For example, if you live in a large city, it will be better to have office buildings as commercial real estate. On the other hand, if you reside in a small town or in an area with factories, you may be better off purchasing and renting out places of business. Profitable commercial real estate will depend on the area you are in; nearly every location will be different. 

It is a good idea to learn about commercial real estate before you jump into it. You need to know what is selling, what is not renting out, and what will work best for you. You should also know the specifics of commercial real estate in your area. Are there laws that govern what you can and can't rent out? Do you have to follow specific codes? Is there a limit to how many commercial buildings you own before you become a principal developer? All of these questions are ones that this book can't answer but will instead need to be figured out in a more local sense.  
By reading this book, you will be able to figure out what type of property will be profitable for you, the amount that particular properties are worth, and the best ways to finance the property. You can also learn the negotiation tactics that pros use so you can make the most out of the process. Figure out how you can benefit from the tax breaks and the deals sometimes found with commercial properties. Try your best, and you will have the best experience possible with commercial real estate. 

Commercial real estate can be a hugely lucrative investment. Not only is it a career that you can benefit from in the now, but it is also something that will bring in residual income for years to come. When you find the right type of property and the right way to market it, you will have less work to do later on, giving you the chance to save for the future. 

Commercial real estate is a lucrative investment, though it takes commitment. You will need to put a lot of work and capital into your commercial real estate, so be sure you are prepared. It is a good idea to try and make sure that you are prepared as much as possible for the things that are going to come in the future. Always do your best and make sure that you are getting money built up and money that you can put aside to be able to contribute to your real estate investment.

GETTING TO KNOW COMMERCIAL REAL 

ESTATE 

COMMERCIAL REAL ESTATE, while fun and exciting, can be a difficult industry, although the cost of entry into the industry is very low. Anyone can be an investor or developer as long as he or she has the drive, moxie, funds, and property skills. Other than obtaining a salesperson’s or broker’s license, anyone can “hang out a shingle” and become a realtor, developer, or consultant. Commercial real estate investment achievement requires an active, rather than passive, thought process to achieve long-term success. This means that property investment and ownership require intensive management skills due to the complex nature of tenant leases and issues; legal aspects of property ownership; divergent property types, land use, and title rights; differing markets for the supply and demand for space; maintenance and capital improvement requirements; and the multitude of equity and debt-funding structures. Several successful industry participants today started out as brokers and small investors buying rental houses or small apartments in their local neighborhood before growing into large commercial property enterprises. 

Real estate is one of the best ways to generate passive income and build wealth. Investing in commercial real estate particularly can become an individual’s highest source of income when done correctly, but many people, including you, probably do not know this or they have no idea  
where to start commercial real estate from. This is exactly why we are going to break down the commercial real estate investment right from the very beginning to the end to help you understand what this goldmine is all about. Before we move ahead, though, let’s answer this question: What is commercial real estate? According to investor.com, commercial real estate is any property that is exclusively used for business activity. That exactly is where the difference between commercial real estate and residential real estate lies. While residential real estate is any property that contains a single or multi-family structure that may not be used for commercial or industrial purpose, commercial real estate is leased out specifically for commercial and business purposes. Note that industrial real estate is not the same as commercial real estate. 

Therefore, a commercial real estate investor purchases or single-handedly develops property solely designed for the purpose of housing commercial tenants. Commercial real estate investment involves the leasing out of this purchased property to businesses that in turn pay rent for the space they are occupying in the property. There are lots of opportunities in the real estate industry for a commercial real estate investor because we can find commercial property all around us and there are several people ready, waiting for a property or part of it to be leased out to them. It is important to know exactly what kind of property counts as commercial real estate before you get out there and start fishing around for investment opportunities. Understanding the different types of commercial real estate property will provide you with better insights into what kind of property you should invest or specialize in. Commercial properties are used for a wide range of purposes, but typically, they can be categorized into five different types: 

Office 

Retail 

Industrial  
Multi-family 

Special purpose 

Mixed-use development buildings are sometimes categorized as commercial properties in the real estate industry, and now, they actually have a growth in demand. These kinds of properties usually have a mix of uses ranging from residential to retail. For instance, a mixed-use property may have apartment units on the upper floors and shopping centers on the lower floors. Before getting started with commercial real estate, you should understand that it is wide apart from residential real estate and so, even if you have been a residential real estate investor before, you must open your mind to learning and acquiring the best strategies for making commercial real estate work for you, too. Next, let’s look at investment opportunities in commercial real estate. 

Investment Opportunities in Commercial Real Estate 

There are two key investment opportunities in commercial real estate. Firstly, real estate investment is distinct from a traditional investment in a way: It holds value as a hard asset, which means it can be a source of income rather than being purchased for the potential selling value like most traditional investments, like bonds. This means that you can always make money from your real estate investment even while waiting for the selling potential to increase. Therein lies the investment opportunities in commercial real estate. 

Commercial real estate investment has a straightforward strategy: There is always an upsurge in demand for real estate in any particular area. So, investors purchase property in this area and then make their income in two ways: First, they lease the property to a commercial tenant who would like to use the property for business in exchange for rent. Secondly, they sell or  
resell the property after it has appreciated over the years. Let’s look at these opportunities more closely. 

*Rental Income Investment* 

Each category of commercial real estate property that we have examined above has tenants. Unsurprisingly, each type of tenant also comes with different property management needs, lease agreements, and different arrangements. For instance, office properties as we have examined above are typically arranged with cubicles and parking decks. Furthermore, the lease agreement usually requires the tenant to pay the rent with a five-to-ten year range in the lease terms. On the other hand, multifamily apartment properties expectedly have families and individuals as tenants with lease agreements that are typically either long term or short term. This may range from a few months to as long as a year. Apartment buildings also have more tenants and leases to manage when compared to office properties. 

*Add Value or Appreciation* 

The second investment opportunity is the increase in the value of a property over the period it is held by the investor. Of course, properties either add value or lose value, depending on the strategy of the investor, over time. Even the best of strategies can’t guarantee gains due to economic variables that could arise and affect the market. But when an investor takes the time to research the market and come up with a strategy using some of the tips you will be getting throughout the course of the book, value appreciation of investment properties will be almost always guaranteed.  

In clearer terms, real estate is a scarce asset because of the inability to create more land, and this scarcity facilitates an increase in demand, which is what real estate investors capitalize on. When demand increases for a property you have previously bought, or in an area around the property, there is every chance you will have tenants willing to pay higher rents or  
potential buyers who will be willing to pay a higher price than you originally invested to purchase the property.  

Time and demand, however, aren’t the only factors that cause the value of a property to appreciate. Skilled and experienced investors also take matters into their own hands by using a “value-add” approach of making improvements to the property to add to its intrinsic value and upgrade its ability to earn more income. For instance, an investor may improve the cosmetic details of a multifamily property, thereby making it an attraction to individuals and families looking to rent an apartment, before charging higher rents. Investing money in renovating and upgrading a property boosts the potential selling price of this property in the future. 

There are two methods of investing in commercial real estate: direct investment and indirect investment. 

**Direct investment** has to do with acquiring direct ownership of physical property, such as becoming the landlord. This type of investment is more expensive and, of course, requires more capital. Direct investment is not suitable for you if you don't already have extensive knowledge of the industry and market, and you can't afford to pay people who do. Commercial real estate (CRE) requires a large sum of capital for investment, so you will, of course, be a high-net-worth individual to invest directly in the market. The model property is found in an area with low CRE supply and significantly high demand, which will serve as a basis for favorable rental prices. The local economy of the area will also affect the value of the CRE property. 

**Indirect investment** involves investing in commercial real estate, acquiring ownership of different market securities like exchange-traded funds, Real Estate Investment Trusts and investing in companies that naturally attend to the commercial real estate market, such as banks.  
Pros and Cons Of Commercial Real Estate Investment 

If you are wondering what the fuss about commercial real estate is and why you should bother investing in it, you probably don't know yet that commercial real estate offers both financial and personal rewards. Some investors acquire commercial real estate properties solely to build wealth and a steady source of income. Other investors utilize CRE for portfolio diversification and tax benefits. You don't have to be either of these categories of investors because everything is achievable when you invest in commercial real estate. 

Here are some of the benefits you stand to gain from commercial real estate (CRE): 

*Higher Source of Income* 

Every commercial real estate investor who has gone about it the right way will tell you that CRE is a sure source of high and steady income. Generally, commercial properties have a higher return on investment (ROI) than residential real estate: Commercial real estate CRE has an average of 6 to 12 percent ROI while single-family residential properties have an average of one to four percent. CRE properties also offer a lower vacancy risk, since the properties tend to have more units. Plus, commercial real estate properties usually have longer lease terms, which eliminates the problem of having to deal with low tenant turnover. 

*Steady Cash Flow* 

Commercial real estate provides a consistent stream of income, thanks to longer lease agreements. For instance, an office space that has been leased on a five-year agreement will provide a real estate investor with a more consistent source of income than that of a single-family building that the lease term is probably one year or below. In addition, CRE properties have  
more units than residential buildings, which means an investor can increase income streams quicker. This is known in the CRE market as a triple net lease. Typically in CRE, tenants also pay the property’s real estate taxes, insurance, maintenance costs, etc. thereby increasing the benefits the owner stands to gain. 

*Low Competition* 

Most real estate investors generally have a preconceived notion of commercial real estate investment as being seemingly difficult, making them unwilling to break into the territory. What this means for you as a commercial real estate investor is that you have relatively low competition. Unlike the residential real estate investment where there is a saturation of investors, commercial real estate provides you the advantage of lesser competition which naturally opens you to more opportunities and of course, gains. 

*Attractive Lease Terms* 

A longer lease agreement is definitely one of the perks of commercial real estate. Commercial real estate properties come with attractive lease terms that provide an opportunity to generate impressive returns on investment and a significant and consistent flow of cash. In most cases, CRE lease contracts are signed for a minimum of three years, which can extend for as many years as possible. This longer lease agreement also ensures less volatility in the market, and a consistent rental income, which potentially mitigates risks related to economic swings. Also, direct investments in CRE, as we have said above, have less volatility in comparison with traditional investments such as stocks and bonds. Since direct real estate investments aren’t publicly traded, the market is rarely impacted by extrinsic events, which tends to affect traditional investment markets.  
Apart from these, there are many more benefits which an investor may stand to gain in commercial real estate investment. These benefits make commercial real estate a better investment market than residential real estate. But as with all things, CRE investment has its disadvantages as much as it has advantages. What are the cons of investing in commercial real estate? 

*Considerable Amount of Time investment* 

Owning a commercial real estate property is quite different from owning residential real estate because with commercial properties, you have a lot more than a single-family property to manage. Commercial real estate investment requires a lot of commitment in terms of time invested because there is no other way to ensure a return on investment. You simply cannot be an absentee landlord sitting somewhere and waiting for your investment to maximize itself. As a commercial property investor, you will probably have to manage multiple leases, annual common area maintenance (CAM), public safety concerns, and other issues that could arise. If you are lucky enough to invest in more than a property, this, of course, means more management work for you. So, it is not advisable to invest in commercial real estate if you don’t have the time to commit to it. Commercial real estate requires as much time investment as capital investment. 

*Professional Help* 

An individual with the “I will do it all myself” mindset simply cannot succeed when it comes to commercial real estate investment. Naturally, you will require the help of licensed professionals to help cater to some of the maintenance issues in a commercial property. Ranging from repairs to emergencies, it pays to have someone to help with some of the issues you will be dealing with. This, of course, means added cost for you. Although this added cost isn’t ideal, you may need to include it in your set of  
expenses from the start so the property can be properly managed and taken care of. You should always remember to consider property management costs when evaluating the amount to use in purchasing a commercial investment property. Averagely, property management companies charge around 5 to 10 percent of rental revenue for management, including lease administration. The best thing is to strategically evaluate your position and understand whether you can manage the leasing and all yourself, or if it will be better to outsource the responsibilities to professionals. 

*Large Initial Investment* 

Naturally, the cost of acquiring a commercial real estate property is higher than what it costs to acquire a residential property in the same local area. Therefore, commercial real estate requires more significant capital for investment. When you acquire a commercial property, you can typically expect some larger capital expenditure to follow suit. For instance, you may have already purchased a commercial property, and a new expenditure comes in the form of repairs or renovations to certain areas of the property. Since commercial properties have more units and expectedly more tenants, you have more facilities to maintain, which translates into more costs for you. The only thing in Commercial real estate investment is that there is always a likely chance that the gain in revenue will outweigh the cost of investment in comparison to when you invest in a residential property. 

*Higher Risks* 

This is not surprising, as markets with more significant Return on Investment (ROI) opportunities as the commercial real estate market typically present higher risks. It is a simple case of "the larger the rewards, the higher the risks." If you are averse to risks, commercial real estate isn't for you because anything can happen at any time. Commercial properties are used for public purposes and, as such, have more public visitors, which  
means more people come on the property every day. These people may get hurt or do something that damages the property. For example, a car may hit a patron in the parking lot, a child may slip on ice in winter, or someone may decide to graffiti the building. Incidents like these are common in commercial properties. To increase your knowledge of the risks involved in commercial real estate investment, let's take a further look at the kind of risks to expect. 

Risks of Commercial Real Estate Investment 

No investment opportunity that offers so many benefits and advantages as commercial real estate comes without risks. To invest in commercial real estate, you must have a solid risk tolerance level. Every investor has a different risk tolerance level. Some investors prefer to invest in high-risk, high-profit properties, while others lean towards lower-risk properties. Therefore, you must know and prepare your mind as an investor for the potential risks CRE is likely to present. Understanding the risks involved in investing in commercial real estate will help you put up a good and successful fight when facing these risks. Let's examine some potential risks an investor is likely to experience. 

*Economic Climate* 

Certain risks in commercial real estate are uncontrollable, including the market and economic climate. As an investor, you have little to no control over factors like financial volatility, unemployment rate, inflation rate, and unexpected geopolitical events that impact the market climate and affect commercial property investment. You need to stay up-to-date with news and details of local, national, and international events that could affect the commercial real estate market. It is quite risky to try to make predictions about what may occur in the future, and it is also dangerous since it makes  
CRE investors vulnerable to reacting to every news in the paper or on the TV. Rather, as an experienced investor, you will instead analytically examine how trends impact commercial real estate over time and then use this to make calculated and informed guesses on whether these variables will have a significant impact in the market, based on the type of commercial property you own. 

*Unexpected Incidents* 

In commercial real estate, certain events simply can't be predicted or prevented because they are out of your hands, including natural disasters, man-made disasters, or criminal threats, all of which can occur at any time without warning. 

*Dynamism of Competitive Environment* 

Changes \= in the commercial real estate market can affect your investment. Technological development and changes in location needs are some of the changes that can impact the commercial real estate market. For instance, the recent willingness of companies to allow their employees to work from home and in non-traditional office spaces has led to a decrease in the need for office spaces. 

Other risks that a commercial real estate investor is likely to face include: 

Business risks: These are risks that impact the bottom line performance of a property. Examples are increased taxes, higher operating costs, and increased labor costs. In addition, significant risks include inflation, regulation changes, rising costs of purchase, and technological advancements, making a business or product go out of date. 

Interest rate risks 

Cash solvency risks  
Supply and demand 

Unstable market changes 

Management risks 

Financial regulatory reforms 

Tax code revisions 

How Do You Respond To Risks In Commercial Real Estate? 

Most CRE risks that have been listed above are out of your control, so the idea is to respond to critical risks only. Other risks usually have minimal impact on your property or the investment goals you set, so they can always be ignored. However, doing this will leave you with a minor subset of risks that, if left unresolved, will affect your business severely. These risks can cause permanent property damage, result in you losing a whole lot of money, or result in property default. The key is to put a strategic set of procedures to always deal with these types of risks. Interestingly, some risks can present you with golden opportunities to make you more money. No matter the procedures you set in place for counter-responding to risks, you will always be affected by two critical factors: how well you do your due diligence, and your ability to set aside emotions when making important decisions. As you read on, you will learn more about due diligence. 

Commercial Real Estate Terms You Should Become Familiar With 

Every industry has technical terms peculiar to it, and a beginner can be identified by their understanding of these terms. To not stand out as a commercial real estate beginner or amateur, you must familiarize yourself with the most important commercial real estate terms. Understanding basic terminologies will go a long way in acclimating you to the market and  
ensuring that you are not cheated while trying to land a deal. These are 10 of the key terms a commercial real estate investor should know: 

*Net Operating Income (Rental Income – Expenses)* 

This term will broadly impact how successful you are with your real estate investments. Net operating income (NOI) is the heart of any commercial real estate deal. It refers to income generated annually from a property after all property expenses have been taken care of, excluding mortgage payment or depreciation. Property expenses typically include any costs that make it possible for you to run and maintain an investment property, such as property management fees, utility, and property taxes. Net operating income doesn't include amortization, depreciation, loan payments, or capital expenditures, and it is usually calculated before tax. The more the net operating income increases, the higher the value of a property becomes, and if NOI goes down, the value of a property also goes down. Note that you can also generate other incomes such as parking lots or laundry from rent on a commercial property. 

*Cash on Cash Return* 

Usually calculated before taxes, cash on cash return is one of the most common terms in commercial real estate because it is, in fact, another word for the return on your investment. Cash on cash is the measure of your property's annual cash flow divided by your property's down payment. 

*Return on Investment* 

Return on investment (ROI), as most people prefer to call it, is the calculated amount you get back from an investment property known as the return, divided by the cost of the property. In more straightforward terms, return on investment is not how much you spend on an investment; rather, it is how much you are able to get out of the property and how fast you can  
get it. Return on investment can be largely impacted by several variables such as renovation costs, maintenance costs, and the amount of loan you originally borrowed to invest in the property. 

*Capitalization Rate* 

The capitalization rate or simply "cap rate" is obtained by dividing the net operating income by an income property's sale price or asking price. A cap rate is the heart of every calculation in commercial real estate because it helps you figure out your potential return on investment before considering other factors like possible mortgage financing. Usually, a lower cap rate means a higher price point, while a higher cap rate means fewer risks. In beginners' terms, the cap rate is the potential ROI if you pay for a property with all cash and no mortgage or loan. 

*Debt Coverage Ratio (DCR)* 

Also known as the debt service coverage ratio (DSCR), the debt coverage ratio (DCR) is used to compare the net operating income of an investment property with its debt service. Investors typically use this terminology with lenders, and lenders use it to calculate if you will generate enough income to pay back your loan. A DCR of 1.15 to 1.35 multiplied by the NOI/annual debt service is usually required by lenders before giving you a loan. 

*Loan to Value (LTV)* 

As a beginner who is considering investing in commercial real estate, the Loan to Value (LTV) is something you will come across repeatedly. Your LTV is determined by the percentage of a property's value or sale price, which is attributed to financing. Therefore, lenders assign a higher LTV to investment properties that have a lower risk. 

*Building Classifications*  
This is the terminology for asset classification, which most property values are determined by. Commercial real estate property falls under Class A, Class B, Class C, and Class D classifications. The market value of a property determines what category it falls under. As we already analyzed in chapter one, Class A properties are located in excellent areas, great aesthetics with significant amenities, and naturally have a higher demand rate. Therefore, you charge the highest rent for Class A properties. Investment properties that fall under Class B, C, or D are less aesthetically appealing than Class A income properties. They are primarily based in locations that aren't quite desirable. 

The higher the class of an income property, the higher in demand it is. One thing about the property classes is that Class A properties usually offer a lower return on investment. In contrast, the lesser classes offer more ROI with more significant risks since they are less appealing in the market. Another thing is that properties in the lower classes require more renovations and maintenance. Therefore, commercial real estate beginners are advised to invest more in Classes B, C, and D properties since they balance risk and return. Make sure you become conversant with identifying various asset classifications for when you have a purchase to make. 

*Price Per Unit* 

The price per unit helps an investor determine the worth of a property and how much to pay for a purchase. For instance, if you have \$100,000 and purchase a property with 10 units, the price per unit would be \$10,000, which you get by dividing the amount you have by the number of units in the building. That is simply your price per unit, and it is at the heart of every commercial property you purchase. There is also the price per square footage that is used when calculating the cost of commercial properties like office buildings, retails, and industrials. Price per unit is usually used for  
apartment buildings. Understanding both price per unit and price per square footage will help you know if a requested for a property is realistic or not. 

*Real Estate Investment Trust (REIT)* 

Real Estate Investment Trust is used for a corporation that controls or finances investment properties. A REIT is similar to traditional investments like stocks. It typically involves buying shares in an investment property and receiving dividends on the rental income generated by the property management company controlling the property. There is a considerable return on investment on REITs for commercial real estate investors, making it an enticing choice. However, REITs are accompanied by some level of risks due to the price volatility vulnerability. Experienced investors prefer to diversify their investment portfolios by buying properties and mixing them up with REIT investments. 

*Lease* 

A lease is a written legal agreement between a property owner, such as you and the tenant. Leases are the lifeline of your commercial property, and there are different types of leases for offices, retail, or residential purposes. 

You now have the ten important commercial real estate tips that you should master as a potential investor. An apt understanding of commercial real estate terminologies will massively impact your rise to the top in the market. They will serve as significant boosts to your investment relationships, negotiations and also give you the confidence you need to discuss prospects with sellers and buyers alike\!

DIFFERENT TYPES OF COMMERCIAL REAL ESTATE INVESTMENTS 

COMMERCIAL INVESTMENT PROPERTY is a capital asset subject to short and long-term leases and fixed or floating leverage that necessitates a long-term holding period of seven to ten years. Longer-term holding periods are required to realize higher rents on lease turnover and amortizing a portion of the property debt. The industry is tenuous in the sense that it is tough to be a successful entrepreneur, whether a broker, developer, investor, or adviser, over a long-term time. The industry is characterized by many boom-and-bust cycles (as discussed below), becoming more frequent and more volatile. Commercial real estate has also become more integrated with the overall capital markets due to the growth and expansion of these capital markets and mortgage-loan securitization and public real estate investment trusts. During the last twenty years, the development of these markets has increased the informational efficiency and data analytics of commercial real estate. Even though integration, data, and increased efficiency are positive, this has led to more volatility. An efficient market is a discounting mechanism whereby asset values are marked to market rapidly, and values can fluctuate quickly and substantially. 

These properties’ sole intent is to be used for commercial and business purposes. Within this classification, there are different types of CRE, including churches, gas stations, schools, gyms, shopping malls, office  
buildings, hotels, hospitals, and hundreds more. Always consider that even when the listing shows property as residential or commercial, the lender always decides what classification best fits. This is an essential factor since, based on this classification, the property may or may not qualify for financing with certain lenders. Therefore, remember always to classify your subject property based on the internal guidelines set by the lender. 

One of the key requirements to becoming a successful owner and investor is timing. Proper timing is essential in any business but paramount in commercial real estate. Timing is critical in entering the industry to acquire real estate at the most opportune point in the market cycle. The most important entry point is when the economy is in recession or a secular downturn (as discussed below), or the lower right-hand quadrant of the graph. This is when prices are low. Huge profits can be made when the economy and real estate markets improve and values increase substantially. When the market is in a downturn or trough, the problem with making investments is that capital is tight as lenders and equity investors pull back and hoard their funds and are afraid to commit money until the market improves. Commercial real estate is a very capital-intensive business, and the ability to invest is a function of the ready availability of debt and equity capital. In recessionary periods, discounted commercial real estate assets are readily available, but capital is not, and therefore, investing in these times is problematic for most, except the largest and most established institutional investors. 

*Income-Producing Real Estate* 

An entity or individual buys income-producing real estate properties to earn income through renting, leasing, or price appreciation. Your primary home residence can never be considered as an income-producing property, even if you lease a portion of your property (basement units, for example). Depending on the state or country where you will conduct your commercial  
real estate finance business activities, local laws and regulations may need to be considered while classifying a prospect property as income-producing real estate. 

Here are some examples of income-producing real estate: 

Office buildings 

Multi-family buildings 

Retail 

Industrial and warehouses 

One important note about this type of commercial real estate is that their ability to service a loan will lay mainly in the cash flow generated by the property itself. 

*Non-Income-Producing Real Estate* 

These properties are those which don't generate rental or leasing income. So, for example, when you own a commercial property, this cannot be considered income-producing since your income source is the business operating in the property and not any rental income. 

Here are some examples of non-income-producing real estate: 

Churches 

Gyms and sports facilities 

Movie theaters 

Gas stations 

Amusement parks 

Day car centers 

Car dealerships 

Marinas  
Hospitals 

Convenience stores 

Cemeteries and funeral homes 

Auto repair shops
