So far, we have learned different types of Real Estate based on their purpose and ability to generate income. Now we are going to learn about CRE based on the kind of tenants occupying the property. This is essential while the lender underwrites a loan application. Based on this classification, the type of tenant may represent a potential liability or an additional assurance of good performance while servicing the loan in the future. 

There are mainly 2 different types of properties under these criteria: 

Single tenant properties 

Multi-tenant properties 

*Single Tenant Properties* 

These are solitary free-standing buildings; they must be built on individual parcels of land and always implies a landlord and tenant relationship, even if it appears the building is owner-occupied. Most single tenant properties often have long-term leases, making a great investment opportunity for developers to secure long-term tenants who typically are franchises. In addition, it is common to find triple net leases (NNN) in place, which become incentives for existing or future ownership. 

*Multiple Tenant properties*  
Multi-tenant properties are typically occupied by more than one tenant and have shorter leases (2-5 years in general). From the lender's standpoint, having multiple tenants is always a plus. Instead of relying on one single tenant as the source of income for this property type, multiple tenants offer the advantage of diversifying the property's income. Keep in mind that the quality of a tenant based on their financial strength and credit profile is something we should always keep under consideration. Multiple tenant properties fall into the commercial real estate category, meaning office buildings, retail, and special-use properties can be a perfect example of properties occupied by multiple tenants. 

Classification of Commercial Real Estate 

*Residential Real Estate* 

These real estate types are meant to become the primary residence of the individual or family purchasing the property. First-time buyers and homeowners looking to buy investment properties to generate rental income are the primary markets for this type of real estate. The type of loan used to finance a single-family residence (owner-occupied) may vary from those intended for investment properties. Under this category, we should consider potential applicants' main profiles: first-time buyers, veterans, second home buyers, and investment property buyers. 

*Residential Real Estate – Rental Property* 

A type of real estate in which an investor purchases properties to make a profit due to a hot housing market or from renovations and capital improvements. Investors who fall into this category often purchase bulk portfolios, meaning the portfolio involves multiple single-family residence properties under one ownership. Financing for this type of deal falls into the commercial mortgage category and will involve a completely different  
process than a residential mortgage. Some residential properties will require special treatment. For example: 

Homes with large portions of farming land 

Homes built with non-traditional materials 

*Retail* 

Retail commercial real estate is the type of structure where some forms of retail constitutes the sole primary usage. This may include various forms of shops, dining, and customer-facing service businesses. In addition, these types of commercial real estate are popular for hosting franchise businesses such as fast food, cell phone carriers, or local businesses. Lately, the mixed use of this property type has attracted businesses like doctors’ offices and other tenants that will typically lease office space. 

*Office Buildings* 

These properties are used primarily to conduct business like: 

Administration 

Clerical services 

Consulting 

Office buildings can hold the same number of tenants. Just like retail, office buildings have seen a recent positive trend involving mixed-use of their leasing space. It's common practice now to have a mix of retail space within the lower levels and office space leased on upper levels. Office buildings are a specialty market because you must be well-informed about your local office demand in order to make a successful investment. 

*Multi-family*  
Multi-family or multi-dwelling units, or MDU, are multiple separate housing units for residential inhabitants contained within one building or several buildings within one complex. A common form is an apartment building. Multi-family units are some of the safest commercial real estate investments since their projected income is easier to assess over a set period of time. Underwriting a multi-family deal requires analyzing rent roll history, financial statements and offering memorandum. The US’s positive trend for multi-family buildings results from first-time buyers opting to satisfy other needs before committing to a long-term mortgage. 

*Industrial Factories* 

Industrial buildings and warehouses and other premises used for manufacturing, altering, repairing, cleaning, washing, breaking-up, adapting, or processing any article; generating power or slaughtering livestock fall under this category. Industrial buildings, same as office and retail, rely on the quality of their tenants to offer a secure investment. Industrial use real estate may not be as glamorous as retail properties, but they have the lowest vacancy rate in the US along with multi-family buildings. A low vacancy rate is always a positive sign when lenders are underwriting a loan/financing request. 

*Hospitality* 

Hospitality is a broad category of fields within CRE buildings that includes lodging, event planning, and additional areas within the tourism industry. As a result, hospitality buildings are an attractive investment for most investors. But you ought to know that it requires deep industry knowledge to nail a successful investment opportunity with this type of commercial real estate. 

*Land*  
Land intended to be used for commercial purposes, including building offices, shops, resorts, and restaurants instead of constructing a residential property. Financing this type of commercial real estate is challenging due to the lack of an existing source of cash flow attached to the subject property. Therefore, it is often required to have a fully developed business plan and a substantial investment of the potential developers, especially when dealing with farming land, mines, or land located remotely and hard to access places. Usually, the loan to value for this type of loan will be very high, and in many cases, a personal guarantee will be required. 

*Special purpose* 

Special purpose property that is appropriate for one type of use or limited use. This type of property has a unique design or layout, uses special construction materials or other features that limit the property's utility for purposes other than the one for which it was built. Gas stations, for example, once the building is vacant, will hardly be used for other purposes than the one used before being vacant. 

Commercial Real Estate Other Kind of Classifications 

From the underwriter's standpoint, it is important to determine the class assigned to our subject property. Even if you have two almost identical properties, it will make a big difference if one of them is Class A and the other one Class B. Lenders will pay special attention to the class of property while assessing the Risk/Benefit factor during their underwriting process. The class our subject property belongs to will determine in great measure our loan amount and loan to value. Think about it: You would not lend the same amount of money for a VW Beetle as the amount you will lend for a Ferrari Testcross. Using Commercial real estate as collateral to secure a loan requires knowledge and understanding of the market where the subject  
property is located and deep knowledge on how to determine what class of commercial real estate belongs to. Let's take a look at the 4 different classes: 

*Class A* 

Investment-grade quality properties with the highest rent; most excellent, newest, and best properties in the best areas; generally owned by institutional investors and fewer than 10 years old. This will be the ideal collateral to secure any type of loan in the commercial lender's world. For an underwriter, this type of property is a treat. But, remember, there is always an exception to any rule. So it could be possible that a Class A may result in bad collateral if hidden circumstances could represent a potential liability for the lender. 

*Class B* 

Buildings are usually older than and not as good-looking as Class A buildings. As a result, investors often target these buildings for restoration. Although the difference in age and appearance could become a factor in establishing the property's value, for the underwriter, a good Class B commercial building with NNN leases in place could be as good as a Class A building with good tenants and no NNN leases. You will often encounter that there is not a set rule or standard about some variables found while underwriting a loan. Combine your knowledge/experience with your common sense. 

*Class C* 

Buildings are the oldest, usually over 20 years of age, located in less attractive areas and often need maintenance. Therefore, even Class C buildings will be considered as solid collateral while seeking financing. Of course, the amounts this type of commercial buildings can secure are much  
lower than a Class A or B, but still can be used to secure a commercial loan. Renovating this type of building is an option to increase your potential rents cash flow, but it will never compare with a Class B redo project as far as ROI %. 

*Class D* 

Bad properties in conflicting locations with high crime rates, legal issues, and/or environmental issues. Class D is much more complicated since most institutional lenders will not consider these properties unless the amount requested is very low and the owner or buyer has a good credit score. Usually, these properties will require a hard money lender in order to obtain financing.  
3 

FINANCING 

COMMERCIAL INVESTMENT ISN'T a venture you can single-handedly finance unless you have a huge load of cash stashed away. If you do not, you need to understand how financing and loans work in commercial real estate investment. Commercial real estate loans differ from residential real estate because it is a larger enterprise. To finance your investment, you must learn the different types of loans available for you; the loan requirements, how to find the best lender for you, and a comprehensive overview of what commercial real estate financing is all about, which is what this chapter aims to explain to you in-depth, with the use of simplified and familiar commercial real estate terms. 

Firstly, know the definition of property loan relative to commercial real estate. Commercial property loans are simply mortgages delegated specifically to buyers of commercial properties. Properties considered commercial produce income and are used only for business activities. This means before you can qualify for commercial real estate loans as an investor, you must be trying to purchase a commercial property only, like retails, office spaces, or multi-family apartments. 

To purchase property, you must be prepared to guarantee the mortgage via collateral or a lien in more technical terms. After getting the mortgage, the  
inability to meet all repayment conditions of the commercial property will result in the creditor or mortgage lender seizing the property. One important thing to note is that commercial investment loans are only granted to businesses and not individuals. So you must first register as a business entity in the form of a corporation or a limited liability company. This is one of the obvious differences between residential real estate and commercial real estate. 

Financing Options 

To understand how financing works in commercial real estate, you must have basic knowledge of the property financial options in the commercial investment industry. You must also be able to tell which of these options is the right one for your investment. Apart from helping finance the purchase of a property, commercial property loans could also help fund any construction projects if there is a need. In addition, you as an investor can leverage your commercial property financing to keep your property fully maintained and operational so you can fully lease them out. Below are different commercial real estate financing options offered by banks, insurance companies, private lenders, pension funds, and the US Small Business Administration. 

*Conventional Bank Loan* 

Banks developed a large part of commercial real estate loans and prefer to lend money to people with strong credit histories. This is also referred to as the traditional commercial real estate financing option. If you have a credit score of at least 660 and plan to work with mid-to-large-sized projects, a conventional bank loan is viable for financing your commercial property deal. Banks do not require you to occupy the property, and they always offer very competitive interest rates, and they lend you the most money at  
the lowest cost. They do require a 20 percent down payment and will likely charge a penalty if the loan gets paid off early. However, conventional bank loans are more suitable for the biggest credit borrowers and businesses with a healthy history of profit-making over the course of a few years. 

*Small Business Administration (SBA) Commercial Real Estate Loans* 

There are two types of loans offered by the US Small Business Administration: the SBA 7A Loan and SBA 504 Loan. These are some of the least expensive loans you will find with a guarantee of repayment of a portion of the loan. SBA-backed loans are helpful because they increase a borrower's credibility and reduce the lender’s risk. The SBA 7A loan is a general-purpose loan that can be used for purchasing and repairing commercial properties. It has a 25-year term for real estate with an interest rate of 7 to 9.5 percent. This type of SBA loan is more beneficial for smaller projects and is the quickest to secure. Although it has a higher interest rate than the 504, it is the most popular loan option between the two. 

On the other hand, you also have the SBA 504, which is more suitable for larger investment projects. With the SBA 504, the borrower is required to bring 10 percent of the loan amount as a down payment, while 40 percent of the loan is sourced from a certified development bank of the SBA. The rest of the loan is sourced from a lender; lenders usually favor loan requests backed by the Small Business Administration. SBA 504 loans work best for commercial investment projects valued at \$1 million or more. 

*Hard Money Loan* 

This is the kind of loan you get from private money lenders and investors, and it is best reserved for when you are looking for a quick solution to some commercial real estate financing problem. Hard money lenders are known for offering short-term loans with a high interest rate, and they do not  
evaluate a loan based on the borrower's credit history. Instead, the loan is assessed based on the potential value of the property. However, qualifying for or accessing a loan with a hard money lender is usually easier than getting from the bank. In fact, as a beginner and a small business, it is best to start your first few commercial real estate investment projects with loans gotten from hard money lenders. Most investors only use hard money loans to quickly finance short-term deals while negotiating a bigger loan with longer terms with a bank. Sometimes, hard money loans are referred to as bridge loans, but there is another source of financing regarded as commercial bridge loans. 

*Commercial Bridge Loans* 

Commercial bridge loans are short-term commercial property loans that you can hurriedly borrow to capitalize on an investment opportunity or purchase a property. Once it is time to repay the loan, you either pay off the whole loan in full or refinance it to a longer-term loan. Bridge loans "bridge the gap" between finding the property and getting an affordable, longer-term financing option. You can get commercial bridge loans either from banks or hard money lenders. The interest rate will differ depending on from whom you borrow. 

*Commercial Real Estate Crowd-Funding* 

A somewhat recent entry to the list of financing options for commercial real estate investors, on crowd-funding platforms, many people lend small amounts of money toward your project. When you add all this money together, you will have a substantial commercial real estate loan ready for your investment. However, these crowd-funding platforms are quite similar to hard money lenders due to the terms and costs. 

*Joint Venture Loan*  
If you are unable to secure commercial loans for your investment project or don't want to bear the risk alone, you can opt for a joint venture loan, where two or more properties apply for financing. With this type of loan, involved parties usually share the risks and returns in the commercial investment equally. However, a joint venture loan ties the involved parties together based solely around one particular property; parties are not required to enter into a true commercial real estate partnership. Joint venture loans are best applied for with people you know and trust at least a little. 

*Online Marketplace Loans* 

Also referred to as "soft money loans," these online marketplace loans have become one of the more popular financing options in commercial real estate investment. They typically involve getting matched with private investors ready to help finance commercial properties on an online marketplace. They are referred to as soft money loans because the interest rates are typically higher than that of the conventional banks but lower than hard money lenders or crowd-funding platforms. You can get shorter-term loans ranging from 6 months to a couple of years on online marketplaces. They are worth a shot when you have a quick short-term project to invest in. These are some of the most popular and reliable means of securing financing for your commercial real estate investment projects. 

How to Qualify for Commercial Real Estate Loans 

To qualify for a commercial real estate loan, you must have some pretty important things in your credentials, or else you may find qualifying for a loan almost impossible. Loan requirements for commercial real estate normally differ depending on the lender you are borrowing from. Here is a brief overview of three important requirements buyers will consider before  
they approve your loan application form and grant you access to a commercial real estate loan for your investment purpose: 

*Credit Score* 

This is usually a basic requirement for any business loan, and commercial real estate isn't excluded. The commercial loans you can qualify for typically rely heavily on your credit score. Naturally, lenders generally prefer to work with investors with a proven record of timely loan repayment and well-managed finances. To ascertain this, lenders consult your credit score and business credit score, respectively. There is no fixed credit score required to qualify for commercial real estate loans, but lenders generally have a progressive range. Hard money lenders are the most accessible loan lenders, and they typically set their required credit score at around 550\. If you have a credit score of 700 and above, you will have access to the best loans, like the SBA and conventional bank loans. 

*Collateral Value* 

Commercial real estate lenders, especially hard money lenders, don't just look at your personal and business finances when considering you for a commercial real estate loan; they also consider the property you are purchasing or renovating. Commercial real estate loans are asset-based loans, which means the property itself usually acts as collateral for the loan. Therefore, lenders consider the collateral value when determining if you qualify for a loan or not. If you are unable to pay off the loan, the lien on the property gives the lender the legal rights to seize and sell off your property to satisfy the debt. 

Since the property is central to the loan agreement and can affect lenders' loan security, lenders will want to make sure they have a complete evaluation and appraisal of the property to see whether it can sufficiently cover the lender's assets. This is an essential requirement for borrowing in  
commercial real estate investment. If you plan to do a complete renovation, lenders will also consider the property's after-repair value (ARV). Some lenders may base the loan amount you qualify for on the ARV of the property. 

*Length and Time of Business* 

Commercial real estate lenders generally require you to know the length of your time in business before they approve a commercial property loan for you. This may be a simple thing, but it can have significant implications on the amount of loan you qualify for. The younger a business is, the riskier a lender considers it. Someone who has a business that has been around for some time has proven that they can manage a business to effectively withstand all the ups and downs that accompany managing a small business. This makes the lender confident that this person will be able to repay a loan. Your business must have been operating for at least two years to have the potential of qualifying for a commercial real estate loan. Lenders sometimes consider management experience too before issuing commercial loans. Having a considerable amount of experience in running and developing a business brightens your application because it proves you are an ideal candidate for a loan. 

Also, take a look at this list of required documents for loan application: 

Purchase contract 

Property address and description 

Property market analysis and business plan 

Budget for property 

Environmental reports 

Existing property’s conditions 

Scope of work for renovation 

Last three years personal tax returns  
Personal credit report 

Records of personal sources of income 

Percentage of owner-occupancy 

Square footage of the property 

Providing a complete application with all necessary documentation gives the lender the opportunity to review your loan application and hopefully approve it quickly. In addition, the more responsive you are to requests for information, the better your chances of getting the lender to approve your loan and charging you a lower loan rate. 

Strategies for Getting the Best Loan 

Even when you understand all the methods and requirements of getting commercial real estate financing, you still need to know the best strategies to apply for a loan and get a good rate. Commercial real estate beginners often assume that the loan qualification process is an easy one because lenders are meant to lend money. This is true in part, but you need strategies to ensure the whole loan application process goes smoothly and make sure you get the best deal available, i.e., friendly loan terms and rates. Apart from preparing all necessary documentation for the loan application, below are some tips for applying for a loan. 

*Have a Proper Plan* 

Lenders usually want to review and understand a borrower's business or property strategy. Why does a borrower want the loan, and how exactly would the loan improve the value of a property or increase the borrower's income? These are the questions you should explicitly answer in your property strategy. Always keep your strategy in mind when meeting with your loan officer. Be straightforward and direct; never waffle from the point  
of the meeting. This will increase your chances since your loan officer will recognize that you have a serious-minded strategy in place. 

*Develop a Corporate Structure Diagram* 

As a real estate investor, you will have multiple, often complex corporate structures ranging from family trusts, associated businesses, and special purpose property vehicles to self-managed superannuation funds. Creating a clear and accurate diagram of your corporate structures gives a lender the opportunity to understand your business structure at a glance, saving you weeks in a reduced loan approval period. 

*Create A Current Rental Schedule* 

A detailed rental schedule with current information about tenants can also play a big part in getting your loan approved. A rental schedule or tenancy schedule, typically detailed information about what tenants pay so that an investor can adequately determine a property's income value, should contain the tenant's form, part of property occupied, type of business, rental rate, the commencement of the lease date, lease expiry date, terms of the lease, and rate of outgoings paid. The tenancy schedule varies by gross rents, turnover rents, and net rents, depending on the commercial property type. 

*Study Comparable Sales* 

Before you apply for a loan, ensure you first study the comparable property assets in locations close to the property. Applying for a loan with comparable property asset information can increase your chances of getting a good loan deal. The lender would see you as someone with specialist knowledge of commercial property and its competitive analysis of its operating environment. These score a level of respect with the lender, and this could be greatly helpful to your loan approval process.  
*Apply With a Property Cash Flow* 

A property cash flow of two to three years can give a lender a lot of information about your property. This could be helpful in letting a lender or loan officer understand your future perspective of the property and your perspective on issues such as tenancy vacancies and capital expenditure. 

*Set Your Terms First* 

Once you provide every requirement needed for the loan request and have a good standing with the lender, never let them dictate the terms of the loan agreement first. Instead, set your terms first. When lenders set terms first, they usually set them so high that it becomes challenging to beat them down. Therefore, tell the lender the interest rate you expect right from the start of the discussions; make sure you tell the lender what establishment fee you will pay, too. Then, the lender would be the one to try to push the terms up. One surprising thing about this is that many lenders don't usually try to push the terms up when the borrowers set the loan terms. 

If you consistently put these tips into practice, you will become a master of securing the best financing for your commercial real estate investment projects. Financing is a critical and integral part of an investment that you should strive to understand as much as possible.  
4 

BUYING / MAKING DEALS IN COMMERCIAL REAL ESTATE 

THERE ARE a lot of things that one has to consider before buying real estate. After all, your real estate will be what takes your business to the next level, and it is the commodity that you will be selling later on to earn your living\! Hence, this chapter includes a list of tips that you should apply while scouting commercial real estate to buy. Consider everything before buying property to ensure that the property is worth selling in the long run. 

Clear Debts and Avoid Amassing New Debts Before You Buy a New House 

You cannot buy a suitable property if you do not have a good credit rating. Your credit rating is a way for people who are looking to sell their property to ascertain whether you are a trustworthy person to sell to or not. After all, because it is doubtful that you will have liquid assets to facilitate buying outright, you will have to use credit to purchase the property, and in order to do so, it is very important that you do not move your money around too much. This means that you should avoid any big purchases starting from six months before you plan to buy any property. Buying things using your credit card racks up debt which lowers your credit score. If you pay your  
debts off quickly, your credit score is raised, but it remains too low until then, making you seem untrustworthy. 

Having a large amount of debt before approaching any property owner that you intend to buy would result in most property owners considering you untrustworthy. The general notion is that you have a lot of debt that you have to pay off, so you might become unreliable while paying off the property. It is also highly recommended that you not get any new credit cards before you approach a seller to buy a new property. A new credit card means a lower overall credit rating because you have not had the chance to pay off any debts on your new credit, so you should avoid it if you can. 

*Get Pre-Approved For a Mortgage* 

First, you need to understand that qualifying for a mortgage is vastly different from getting approved for a mortgage. This is because the stamps of approval or qualification have very different connotations and thus say different things about your financial reliability. It is very easy to get pre qualified for a loan. So easy that telling a potential seller that you are pre qualified won't boost their opinion of you in any significant or meaningful way. Getting pre-approved for a mortgage, on the other hand, is an entirely different matter. This is because the process of getting pre-approved is much more complex and time-consuming, and not everybody ends up getting approved for a mortgage or a loan. If you are qualified and you head to the bank to get a loan, the approval process starts. 

Essentially, getting approved is impossible unless you have an excellent credit rating. To get approved for a mortgage, you need to prove that you will pay the mortgage back without missing payments. When a bank pre approves you for a mortgage, it has essentially already granted you the mortgage. In addition, the executives at the bank will have looked into your financial history and will have ascertained to a large degree how financially  
reliable you are. For these reasons, a seller will be more willing to sell to you if you are pre-approved for a mortgage. Hence, you can save yourself a lot of time and effort by planning your purchase and getting yourself pre approved for a mortgage before you approach any prospective sellers. 

*Mind Your Property Lines* 

The survey is one of the most essential parts of the pre-buying process. It points out any areas of concern and ensures that you head into this purchase with your eyes open, aware of anything that might cause problems in the future. uring the survey, focus on the property lines. Having indistinct, undefined, or irregular property lines can result in problems if left unresolved before the house has been purchased. The deeds must have been transferred to your name. If your property lines overlap with those of a neighbor, there can be legal trouble. Additionally, property lines encroaching on an area that should technically belong to your neighbors is an ethical offense that can very quickly turn into a legal one. 

In order to avoid lengthy and unnecessary complications with your home, monitor the property lines before your property has been purchased. Potential legal problems are worth fixing before the property is yours. Property lines can also cause issues with property taxes. If your property lines extend to an irregular shape and you are unaware of this, you might end up paying more property tax than you are aware of because it is calculated using square footage. Hence, it is important to know your property lines to get an exact estimate of how much property tax you will pay instead of getting an unpleasant surprise on tax day. 

*Don't Wait for the Right Time* 

There is no way to predict the commercial real estate market, meaning that you absolutely cannot wait for the right time in order to purchase a property you want because there might not be one. This is one of the major problems  
that people find with the commercial real estate market. Trying to time the market can only result in you missing out on opportunities. 

To make it big in commercial real estate, you need to be assertive and confident, and you need to know how to market things. Hence, the best thing to do if you want to make good money in commercial real estate is to look hard, find a property that you love or you think you can fix up well, and buy it. If you like a property, this means that the property has several likable qualities. This means that many people will agree with you and see the same positive attributes in this property. Commercial real estate is cyclical. When it goes up and when it goes down is entirely random, so don't miss out on your dream purchase because of the way it is acting. 

*Don't Judge a House by Its Size* 

This is a common rule in the commercial real estate business: Never buy the biggest property on the block. This might seem odd to you. After all, everybody wants the biggest property on the block\! Everyone wants to use that mansion to lord over the rest. So the property that is the most expensive can be sold for the most as well, right? Your logic is sound, but it doesn't take into account that everybody wants the biggest property, but very few people ever end up buying it. This means that if you buy this enormous property, you will severely limit your potential buyers due to the simple fact that not many people will be able to afford to buy it, no matter how much they want it. 

This also means that your property is never going to appreciate much. Since the price is already so high, there is a minimal amount of growth space that you get for the price, no matter how much you do to it. This contrasts with properties in the same neighborhood, which are worthless. Therefore, it would be wiser to buy a smaller, maybe even the smallest and most neglected property in the neighborhood if it has big potential. Fixing the  
property up and making it competitive will not cost nearly as much as buying the bigger property, but the returns you will get from selling this smaller property will be much more significant. Hence, unless you plan to use it instantly yourself, never buy the biggest property in the neighborhood. 

*Don't Treat Mortgages like Rent* 

Paying off a mortgage does, in a lot of ways, seem like rent. After all, you are paying a monthly payment that can be similar in amount to rent. So what makes a mortgage so different from rent? Why don't people just save up for a down payment and buy property all the time? To understand this difference, you will have had to own property some time in your past. The major difference between renting a property and owning one is that several costs are not included in your monthly payment. These include your maintenance costs, since you are the landlord. There is nobody but you who will fix up your property when something breaks, and your monthly, bimonthly, or biannual payment to the property association. 

Many rentals also do not come with utility bills, a fixed amount for which is most often included in the rent itself. However, if you own the property, you will pay the bills. Additionally, you will pay a significant amount of property tax if you own a property, something that you would not have to do if you were simply renting it. Hence, it is vital that you keep these additional expenses in mind when buying a property. Don't just think that you are going to have to make monthly payments and nothing beyond them. Doing this is shortsighted and will result in financial problems that could decrease the value of your property. 

*Go for Your Instincts, Not Emotions* 

A lot of people end up buying a house because they fall in love with it. It might remind them of their childhood homes, or it might have a feature that  
they have always wanted. This is perfectly fine if you intend to live in the property, though it is highly not recommended. However, if you are planning on selling a property, buying based on your emotions is one of the worst things you could do. Remember, you are not planning to marry the property you are buying; you are planning to sell it. 

The main driving factor behind your purchase of a property should be instinct. Instinct will make you look at a property, even one completely broken down, and see it for what it will be worth in the future. It makes you see the neighborhood around the property as clean, safe, and a place where people would want to live in the neighborhood, which makes the buy worth it in the long run. In essence, instinct allows you to see the bigger picture. Emotions make you want to buy it for the color or the floor tiles; it has absolutely nothing to do with how much money you can make off the property after fixing it up and letting it appreciate for a few years. Be smart about the property you are buying. 

*Use a Home Inspector* 

You might consider a property inspector for your property but have second thoughts because it costs a couple hundred dollars. However, these couple hundred dollars might just end up saving you thousands of dollars in the long run. Commercial real estate is about making good purchases and avoiding bad ones. You know what sells and what doesn't, but you aren't a property expert, which means that many things might be wrong with a place you will have missed, which could devalue your property if you are not careful. A property inspector's job is to perform a thorough inspection of a property and find any faults. If they do not find any, you can rest assured that a professional has deemed your property free of any problems in the future.  
However, if an inspector finds faults in the property you are thinking of purchasing, you can use them to leverage a lowered buying price from the seller. This is very important because if you tell the seller about the problems yourself, the seller could discredit your findings, saying that you are not qualified. However, if a professional property inspector relays these problems for you, you will have a real reason to buy the property for a much lower price than you would otherwise. Additionally, getting a professional inspection done is a way to ensure that the property you are buying is being bought on instinct or emotion. If you see something in the property, the chances are that the inspector will see it, too. There is no better way to get an objective opinion on the property you intend to buy. 

*Be Careful With Your Opening Bid* 

The opening bid is one of the most essential parts of buying commercial real estate. Unfortunately, there is a lot of misconception around the opening bid. First and foremost, many people tend to think that the lower the price they offer in the opening bid, the better the offer they will get in the long run. This is not true. Offering too little with the opening bid might end up offending the seller, which means that they would not be willing to sell you the property later on. If you are looking to make a competitive opening bid, there are two main factors that you need to keep in mind. First and foremost is what you can afford. You are the one who will pay, so why offer something that you couldn’t? This is also important because it will prevent you from overbidding. 

Keep its worth in your eyes in mind. The two numbers will not be far apart if you have done your homework by keeping your credit score up and getting yourself pre-approved for a mortgage. Hence, unless you are shopping for a property in an area outside a reasonable budget, you should be able to find a happy medium and haggle away from there. You should also look into whether the property taxes for the property have been paid or  
not. Many properties have unpaid property taxes, which is information that can be used to leverage a lower price. 

*Research the Neighborhood* 

Suppose you are looking for property to set up a business such as an eatery, a grocery store, a bar, a clinic, or so on. In these instances, when one buys a property, they don't just do it for the property itself. Another very important factor that affects people who are thinking of buying a property is the neighborhood the property is in. People want a safe environment for their children; they want a place that is respectable and accepting. Hence, it is important that you stake out the neighborhood before you buy a property. Many neighborhoods look good in the middle of the afternoon, but once the sun sets, the block completely changes. Nobody wants to live in an unsafe area, so you need to do your homework. As a result, you may end up spending money on a great property that no one will want to buy because they don’t think that the neighborhood is worth the quality of the property, no matter how high the quality of the property itself is. 

First, sweep the neighborhood. Check to see how far the nearest shops are, and pay close attention to the schools. About a fifth of your property's value depends on the quality of the schools nearby, so you can use bad schools as leverage to lower the price or as a reason not to buy at all. To be sure of the neighborhood, come back and see what's going on at random times during the day. You could even drive through the neighborhood on your way to your job every day. 

Buying Commercial Properties via Bank Repossessions and Auctions 

Buying commercial properties through bank repossessions means buying properties that were once financed by banks but were defaulted on by the  
owners. Because of this, the bank takes the property back into its possession before selling it to someone else. Although bank repossession isn't something you wish for as a commercial real estate investor, it sure is something you can take advantage of to get some outstanding commercial investment deals. Most bank-owned commercial properties are for sale; however, it is still essential that you get some professionals to help you look into the property with a thorough investigation so you can submit a competitive bid for the property. 

Before searching for commercial bank properties, you must first recognize the type of property you are looking to purchase; this will help tailor your search and make it more specific. Once you know the type of commercial property you are looking for, get a list of banks' websites so you can check them up, as banks typically list the properties they have for sale on their websites. You can do this using a search engine; simply go to your favorite search engines, such as Bing or Google. Then, type the name of the bank and Real estate owned (REO) into the search engine; immediately, you will see the results of some bank websites where their REOs are listed. For example, if you are looking for REO properties owned by Wells Fargo, you go to Google and type "Wells Fargo REO," and this brings up a result of the list of commercial properties Wells Fargo has up for sale. US Bank, Wells Fargo, and BMO Harris are some of the banks with REO properties in the United States. You may do a local search according to banks in your area. 

You can also find commercial bank properties for sale on Loopnet, a valuable website with information on listings for bank-owned commercial properties in the US. To access the listings, sign up to be a member to access to the site's premium bank-owned commercial property listing. The listings will typically contain the size, price, and type of commercial property. Banks usually try to auction real estate-owned properties before listing them for sale, so you should also check out local auctions around  
you. Monitor upcoming auction events in the newspaper. Most properties displayed at auctions, however, are usually never bid on, so going to auctions is just a way of looking out for good commercial properties on the market sooner or later. To raise your chances of getting REO properties for sale, you should also work with a trained commercial real estate broker. An experienced broker is more liable to have listing information that may otherwise be hidden from you. If you already have a broker, make sure they are competent. 

When buying a commercial property from the bank, make sure you are familiar with the property. As is standard, the location of the property should be first and foremost in your mind. Why was the initial owner unable to complete the loan repayment? Was the property located in an area with little or no potential and tenant appeal? The most appealing properties to tenants are those in a location with access to public transportation, visibility from the road, sufficient foot traffic, and nearby businesses. Next, consider if the companies close to the building are compatible with your target clientele's businesses, or do they pull in different clients? If the real estate-owned building is an apartment or multi-family, find out things like the condition of neighboring properties and location of schools, hospitals, and grocery stores. After this, do a standard physical assessment of the property. Do not assume that this is unnecessary because it is a bank-owned property. Next, go with an inspector and contractor to determine the level of repairs needed and just how much these repairs would cost. Since these buildings are usually occupied, or they are abandoned, there will always be some repairs, so ensure you are thorough in your property inspection. 

Talk to the bank about the current tenants. Ask about the number of units in the building, the number of rented ones, and how long each tenant has occupied them. Also, ask for the rent-rolls, which contain information about the complete number of tenants, names, and the lease terms. If the bank isn't  
willing to provide this information, you could take it up a notch and contact the former owner; ask them for the information you need. Then, before you pay for the purchase, analyze your rental income potential. What can you charge for rent? The bank, i.e., the current landlord, may not be charging a market rent, so do some research on what landlords in that particular area are charging. You can either collaborate with property management companies or go online to get this information. Several sites offer information—for example, padmapper.com. Also, ensure you do a comparative study of nearby buildings. Properties that are in a much better location will probably charge higher than the other properties. Importantly, ensure you ask the bank for available financial records. Since the property was foreclosed, there is a chance that the complete financial record won't be public. Nevertheless, work with your broker and the available records to help calculate the right bid amount for the commercial property. 

Now, it's time to make an offer for the real estate-owned (REO) property. You will need to work with your team of lawyers, accountants, and mortgage brokers. You can opt to apply for a loan from the bank, from which you are buying the property; they may oblige, or they may not. They may be the ones to offer to finance the purchase, but if they don't, check any of the means of financing we looked at and choose a suitable one for the transaction. Get all the necessary documents, and apply for a loan before you work on calculating the bid. 

With your broker, assess the bank's sale price for the property. Is it too high? Or is it too low? If it seems to be too low, that probably means there is something wrong with the property, and the bank is looking to have it offloaded. Next, ask your broker to study the real estate market in proximity and determine what a fair sale price would be. As a savvy investor, you may want to begin the offer with a low bid amount in a move to get the bank to negotiate. Know every bank is different; most banks are not interested in  
getting anything below top dollar, even if the property was foreclosed. Therefore, ensure you begin bidding with your best price. Next, ask your lawyer to help draft a purchase and sale agreement, which will be submitted to the bank. Since the agreement will become a legally binding contract if accepted, you should use a lawyer. 

Send it to the bank as soon as it is drafted. Include a feasibility contingency to review expenses, leases, income, market potential, and other relevant issues before purchasing the property. Include an expiration date in your offers to determine how long you will have to wait for an acceptance or a counteroffer from the bank. Keep in mind that banks rarely respond to offers quickly. If the bank responds with a counteroffer rather than an acceptance offer, you will proceed to the negotiations. Typically, they will send their purchase and sale agreement, which might not wholly be of benefit to you. Review the purchase and sale agreement with your broker and lawyer but know that banks are normally hard negotiators even when there is a motivation to sell; bring in your best negotiation skills. Once you and the bank agree, proceed to close the deal. 

*Advantages of Bank Repossessed Properties* 

There are many pros and cons of purchasing a foreclosed property; these benefits make purchasing REO commercial properties give you the possibility of getting very good deals, especially when the amount owed to the bank is less than the property’s market value. 

Banks with foreclosed properties on listings usually do not look to profit from the sale; they just want to recoup their losses. You could find yourself a good bargain if you purchase a property listed as REO. 

The bank is a VAT vendor, so there is no need for transfer duty payable on a foreclosed property.  
Banks require the municipal accounts to be up to date, so you don’t have to worry about taking on somebody else’s municipal debt. 

*Disadvantages of Bank Repossessed Properties* 

Like we already said, most repossessed commercial properties are usually in very poor condition, and they always require some level of renovation. As the buyer, you will need to consider the cost of renovation on top of the purchase price to ensure that the deal is a good bargain or a potential money trap. Location is primary to any commercial real estate deal, so never compromise on location just to get a seemingly good deal. 

If the property has tenants, you, as the new owner, will be responsible for vacating the tenants from the property. Sometimes, this may be as simple as giving the occupants a notice, or worse, it would be a long process of legal eviction, which spells more stress for you. 

When purchasing a foreclosed property, there will probably be some hassle, and you should know if the whole stress is worth your while. 

How Do Bank Repossessions Work? 

When a commercial property owner can no longer meet their loan terms and are in substantial arrears, the bank takes legal action by serving the owner a court summons, taking judgment, and attaching the property eventually. If the homeowner is still in arrears by the time of attaching the property, the bank will request the court sheriff to provide property images and details at a public auction event. At the auction, a bank representative is entitled to purchasing the home if the bids aren't enough to cover the  
outstanding fees owed to the bank. Thus, the home becomes a repossessed property or property in possession once it is bought back by the bank at the auction. Immediately the bank purchases the property at the auction; it becomes the registered legal owner of the property. In this case, the bank either puts the property for sale to recoup their losses or rents it back to the former owner on a month-to-month lease agreement. 

Tips for Purchasing Commercial Real Estate at Auctions 

Buying properties at auctions is an excellent way of getting huge returns on your investment, so use some of these tips to help you through the process of purchasing properties at auction events. 

Prepare the cash. Most action events require you to close the deal within a short time after the auction, usually within 30 days. Unfortunately, this makes it impossible for you to get traditional financing to purchase an auctioned property. So ensure that you have a credit line available or a lender willing to loan you on credit once the auction closes. Generally, the purchase agreements in auctions are not open to financing contingencies, so if you can't prepare the cash for closing, you are at risk of losing your earnest money. There is also the liability of damages. 

Take property tours. When it comes to auctions, this is usually the only time a potential buyer gets to see or inspect a property, so you should never miss the property tours. Most auctions have specified dates available for tours. During the tour, see if the property has tenants; you can ask about the units and issues they are facing. Also, look out for potential improvements and repairs. 

Request to know the format of the auction. Familiarize yourself with auction types and definitions: online vs. sealed bid, reserve vs. absolute  
auction, and more. The type may depend on the company holding the auction. 

Be aware of insider bidding. Many times, auction companies get insiders to bid up a property on the auction being held. This is done to inflate the bidding price of the property artificially. Do not be pressured into bidding at a higher price than you can afford. 

Get experts to represent you at auctions. Have your team of brokers, attorneys, accountants, inspectors, and contractors ready to go over all the materials presented and become comfortable before purchasing. Make sure everyone on your team is good at what they do. 

Never infuse emotions into a purchase. It doesn't matter whether you like a property or not; if the deal isn't right, it isn't right. Know when you reach your limit; if you have a limit set, don't get too competitive and overly excited by trying to win the auction just to win. Auctions are usually very exciting; coupled with the possibility of a strong return on investment, they may overwhelm you. Recognize and stick to your limits because there are always better deals waiting if this one doesn’t work out. 

Auctions and repossession may be good sources of good commercial real estate deals. However, it is important to know when to avoid making these types of deals. Before you make an offer for auction and repossessed bank properties, make sure you have adequately done your research. If it doesn’t seem like a good enough deal, do not hesitate to move on to the next deal. 

Staying Up to Date with Trends in the Market 

Keeping up with news and trends in the real estate market is a way of gaining insights into the country's state. When you follow trends in the commercial real estate market, it allows you to see other aspects of the  
nation's economy and social progression. Therefore, to be a savvy real estate investor, follow and stay up-to-date with trends in the commercial industry and the general market. Here are the best websites and online news outlets to help you on top of the news and trends in the commercial real estate industry: 

Forbes: An established site about wealth and finance with specific sections dedicated to real estate and commercial real estate. Realty Times: Here, you will find tips for improving your property and how to make the best financial decisions when buying and selling. 

RIS Media: Offers insightful information on government acts relevant to the real estate industry and social acts. 

Realtor.com: This is a source of social internet information with helpful posts centered on current trends and events. 

Entrepreneur: Everything business, ranging from making money and doing smart business. They primarily concentrate on real estate investment facts, news, and trends. 

Making Deals 

If you are starting out, it feel like you're getting a good deal over a property because it has a low price. But, buyers beware. A lower price on the property could signal problems, and you will need to ensure that you will be truly obtaining a package before you decide to flip the business. 

How to Find Great Deals on Commercial Real Estate 

One of the questions that commercial real estate beginners have is how to find great deals. The answer is always the same: There is no magic solution.  
You need to use a variety of methods. 

*Ads in Newspapers* 

Imagine someone who owns a commercial real estate building. Chances are, you are not thinking about someone who is twenty years old. Most likely, in your mind, you have a picture of an older person. The older someone is, the higher the chances that their life does not revolve exclusively around the internet. This is why you want to make sure that you pay attention to local newspapers ads. You will find many owners willing to sell their properties due to health issues, retirement, and family circumstances. Often, properties that you will find in small ads will turn out much more lucrative than those advertised on popular websites or big banners. Big ads are usually placed by real estate agents or by people who want to attract a lot of attention to their property, which to you means a lot of competition. People who place small ads usually avoid significant marketing expenses, dealing with real estate agents, and paying all commissions. They want a quick deal and are looking for someone who will give them what they are looking for without hassle. 

*Commercial Real Estate Brokers* 

Commercial real estate brokers are another great source of leads for deals on commercial real estate. Ensure that you are on the mailing lists of both large and small commercial real estate firms in your area. You also want to stay in touch with agents that work by themselves. Arrange a few meetings, inform them about what you are looking for, and keep in touch to make sure that they remember you and tell you about available properties. A lot of people tend to stay away from real estate agents because they want to avoid commissions. In most cases, it is the seller of a property who pays the commission. Brokers will have information about the people who have  
decided to use a broker. Therefore, you are not losing anything by dealing with a commercial real estate broker when looking to acquire a property. 

Many commercial real estate investors choose to stay away from agents who are also commercial real estate investors themselves. Such investors think that the agent-investor will not show them any good deals and keep all the best properties to themselves. In reality, there are several reasons why an investor-agent may choose to pass on a property. It may be that they do not have enough money, or that they do not specialize in a certain kind of commercial real estate or don't have the right tenants for the property. At the same time, an investor-agent will not lose your time talking to you about deals that make no sense. Your work with an investor-agent may result in a beneficial partnership. 

*The Internet* 

While we did start this section by discussing newspaper ads and dealing with real estate agents, we are not dismissing the internet or its power. The internet can be an excellent resource for commercial real estate leads and deals. Today it is possible to find listings, communicate with tenants, sellers, buyers, and agents, submit offers, conduct your research, apply for loans and insurance and even manage a property through the internet. You can explore and invest in markets located in different parts of the country far away from each other. Therefore, regularly visit the websites that have commercial real estate listings. Unfortunately, the problem with the internet is that it is easy to find listings for you and your competition. However, even with this, is it worthwhile to visit the websites often. 

*Being Attentive Every Day* 

A great source of leads is always being on the lookout for what is going on around you. For example, you may notice a "For Rent” sign suddenly pop up when a property owner is trying to see whether they can rent the  
property without going to a real estate agent. A sign that says "For Sale By Owner "is a surefire way to know that no real estate agent is involved in the deal. Often you will also see signs that say that the building is for sale or lease. This means that the owner can't find a good tenant and is willing to settle for either selling or renting the building. Such signs indicate that there is a definite opportunity for a great deal. 

When driving or walking around, you will also see buildings that do not have any signs. Such buildings are usually in awful condition, have unmaintained lawns, lots of trash, and dusty windows. You can go to the county's assessor office, find the owner, and inquire about buying the property. It is also a great idea to take different routes when commuting to your office or picking up and dropping kids off at school. Do not stick to one road or one way to go. Take different routes at different times and pay attention to what is going on. 

*Word of Mouth Advertising* 

While all the methods for attracting clients that we have discussed above work effectively, the best method is when the tenants seek you themselves because they have heard about you from their friends, acquaintances, or connections. This is why you want as many people as possible to know that you are on the lookout for deals. For example, your aunt may not be interested in becoming a tenant in a commercial property. She may also not come up with ten people that you should talk to. However, in six months, you may hear from her dentist, who learned from her about the fact that you are in the commercial real estate business and now wants to talk to you. 

How can you accomplish that? First, talk to more people. Watch less mindless television and cut the time that you spend on activities that do not bring you any pleasure and do not help you get closer to your goals. Next, take out your business card and look at it. Most likely, you have your name  
in big letters and then, in small letters, something similar to “Vice President.” The first thing you want to do is change your title to “Commercial Real Estate Investor.” Understand is that no one really cares about your name. Finally, you may want to add a tagline to your business card, such as “I buy commercial buildings and help commercial tenants find perfect spaces for them.” 

How to Analyze Deals 

You see the building and its condition. You have a great opportunity. The owner of the property has been around for years and has a great reputation. However, not all commercial deals are this straightforward. For example, a commercial property may have a number of titles, plot ratios, leasable premises, and tenants on a number of leases. This is the case where you would want to perform due diligence on a property. Due diligence means finding enough information about a property to be confident that the property is a good deal. It includes a review of financial records, property titles, and anything else relevant to the property. 

The first step should be to verify that the seller is the actual legal owner of the property. After that, the sellers can and often do perform due diligence on the buyers. The main thing they are interested in is the buyer's ability to purchase the property. There are two types of due diligence that you want to perform. The first one consists of items that are hard to describe in numbers, such as street appeal, good highway access, how close the property is to an airport, or how much foot traffic the property gets. This last piece of information is an example of a number you can find out, but it's hard to decide what to do with it. 

Fortunately, most of these items will be reflected in the market trends for the area. For example, properties with great transportation options and high  
volumes of foot traffic usually rent and sell for a higher amount than properties without these features. While there is no formula to include all these factors into the equation, you need to become aware of the trends in your area to make intelligent decisions. Learn the total land area, total square footage of the building, taxes, and insurance rates in your area. 

Sending Oers to Sellers and Successfully Negotiating a Deal 

An offer in commercial real estate investment is a written declaration of intent sent to a seller to make your interest as a serious buyer known. It can be pretty exciting and frightening to send your first offer to purchase a commercial property. Make sure you get everything right, including the legal parts. Here is a breakdown of the steps you are meant to follow when making an offer for a commercial property. 

Firstly, there are two ways to make your offer: through a letter of intent or a purchase contract. As a newbie, you probably won't know which method to use. Usually, the letter of intent is used to notify the seller of your interest in the property as a serious buyer who is willing to close a deal fast with all the terms and price stated in the letter as long as both of you can work through all the details to complete the transaction entirely. On the other hand, the purchase contract is the final document that all the parties involved in a transaction sign to create a binding contract and agreement. It contains all of the legal clauses and addendums with a detailed explanation of the transaction. 

Many investors would rather present an offer with a basic letter of intent first since they don't want to put in the time and effort to create a purchase contract for a property. So, a letter of intent is used to test the waters. The letter of intent (LOI) demonstrates your interest in a property with the terms you are proposing, and if the seller is interested in your terms, you can talk  
some more and see if you can both arrive at a deal. To make the seller understand that you may be interested in purchasing the property, work with your attorney to draft a letter of intent containing some clauses that create a good faith expectation on both your and the seller's sides. 

A letter of intent is more advisable for presenting the first offer, especially because of the simple manner in which you can get the most important points across to the seller. The seller may find it quite convenient reading a simple one-page letter of interest than a 10-15 pages documents with all the legal clauses and terms that would make them bring in their attorney for a look together; the letter of intent is much easier to read and agree with immediately than a detailed purchase contract. However, the disadvantage of a letter of intent is that you don't have a legally binding contract. The seller may decide to cancel or go with another buyer at any point during the discussions. Therefore, you must make an effort to convert a letter of intent to an actual contract as soon as possible, especially if the property is one you are really interested in. When drafting the letter of intent for sending your offer, use a state-approved commercial contract for buying and selling real estate so the seller can see that you are in for serious business, as most buyers feel more comfortable with the state-approved commercial contract. 

Once you have sent an offer, you may begin negotiations, which is where you need some pretty important tips to help you ensure you are on top of the game. Good negotiation skills are integral to commercial real estate transactions. When you have a motivated seller and some vital negotiation skills, the seller will likely agree to the terms and prices you propose. In addition, how good you are at negotiation could determine whether a buyer continues a transaction with you or moves on to another interested buyer. 

Tips For Negotiating A Deal  
Negotiations can be pretty intimidating when purchasing your first commercial property. Deal making and negotiations are more of art than science, and you have to master this art. There are tenets of negotiations that you stand to benefit from as a commercial real estate investor. Here are five important tips for successfully negotiating a deal: 

*Do Your Homework* 

Before you meet for a negotiation with a seller, ensure you already know everything there is to know about the property, the seller, and other related information that highlights what you have in front of you. Be familiar with all the facts. 

*Have a Plan* 

It is important to have a game plan before you start negotiating. Know the key points you want to target during meetings with the seller and the outcomes you want these meetings to have. You should already have the price, terms, and possible changes outlined before the negotiations start. Be straightforward and specific. 

*Stay in Control* 

Never let the seller dictate the tune of the negotiation; always be in control of the discussion because you are the one who needs the deal. Brush up on your communication and persuasion skills, and learn how to handle negotiations yourself. Also, never let anybody else do the negotiations for you; it should be your responsibility. If you are going to let someone else handle the negotiations for you, this should be your lawyer or broker, and you must ensure their competence level is top-notch. 

*Find Out the Seller’s Motivation*  
This doesn’t mean asking them a direct question about why they are selling the property. Rather, it means listening and looking subtly for clues through the course of your discussions. Every investor wants the best possible deal they can get, and a seller's motivation plays an important part in determining how great a deal is. Bridge the imaginary gap between the seller and yourself, and don't be afraid to ask questions politely if you feel like they aren't telling you anything. 

*Be Empathetic and Accommodating* 

Usually, empathy isn't considered part of the skills required to succeed in the commercial real estate industry. However, being empathetic about your counter-party’s needs and goals can come in handy. Talk to your brokers. Accommodate the a seller, especially if you know why they are selling the property. Make sure they are settled in before you begin the meeting; be encouraging, motivating, and easy to work with. Let them feel your empathy and sincerity. No matter how heated the discussion gets, maintain an air of pleasantry. Sellers prefer to work with people who make working with them as easy as possible. After successfully negotiating and mutually agreeing to a deal, the next step is to close the deal and become the owner of your new property. Let’s take a look at how to close a commercial property deal successfully. 

Properly Close A Deal 

If negotiations go well and a seller accepts your offer, the next stage is closing a deal, which takes between 30-90 days. Until the closing process is over, it is not ideal for getting over-excited about the deal. There are important actions to take to ensure that closing goes as smoothly as it can. Aside from signing the closing documents, it is also necessary for you to make sure the purchase is legal, final, and with a legal seal of approval.  
Before you can officially call the property yours, you will still need to pay a considerate amount of attention to the whole process. 

*Escrow* 

Creating an escrow agreement between you and the seller is the first step to take after an offer is accepted. This is quite similar to a residential closing process where both parties have an escrow agreement to ensure seriousness and trustworthiness with the sale process. In escrow, a third-party neutral to the whole transaction holds the closing fund in an account inaccessible to both you and the seller. Until all criteria in the deal agreement are met, the money will stay put in the escrow account. If one party decides to exit the deal through all the terms stated in the agreement, the funds can also be released. The criteria to be met are usually agreed on by both the buyer and the seller. Commercial property deals are even more closely monitored by the buyer, seller, and escrow agent during escrow than residential real estate deals. Few regulations prevent one party from hurting the financial security or reputation of the other, so both parties must work toward protecting their investments. Title agents usually act as the neutral third party. 

*Titles and Closing Documents* 

Each party participating in the deal must apply their best efforts in protecting themselves from being played. This process of doing their best is referred to as due diligence. As the buyer, you should ask the seller to present relevant documents to verify that the property is insured and in accordance with local laws and ordinances. With their attorneys, both buyer and seller should thoroughly review the contract of sale and ensure that every detail has been executed with no outstanding ownership or legal disputes. 

*Renegotiation*  
While inspecting the documents, property and generally doing your due diligence, talk to the seller, ask questions, and start renegotiation if you find something out of place. Renegotiations are important for reviewing parts of the clauses that you are no longer comfortable with based on whatever you notice in the review of the necessary documentation. 

*Signing of Documents* 

After thoroughly reviewing all the documentation to ensure no stones are left unturned, the documents are ready for signature and notarization. Apart from the title and insurance policy, you should also remember to take possession of all leasing documents; this is to allow you to benefit from them while being held responsible for any breach of contract subsequently. An attorney and the title agent should also review all documentation to ensure nothing is missed in the whole process. 

*Coordinate Closing Requirements* 

Often, when closing nears, new, unexpected issues may arise and need attention. The reason why problems often arise towards the end of closing is reliance on an independent third party and providing certifications and showings dated very close to closing. As closing approaches, ensure that your broker, attorney, and other representatives remain available to respond to possible changes, demands, and arising circumstances. 

*Closing Day* 

The closing day is when you officially become the owner of the new commercial real estate of the property. A part of the closing document on the closing day is a quitclaim or special warranty deed; this is the official document that transfers ownership of a property from a seller to the buyer. A title affidavit usually accompanies the deed. Commercial real estate investment has a more complicated, complex, and lengthy closing process  
than residential real estate. Since there are few regulations by the government regarding the process, both parties involved must do everything in their capacity to structure the deal, the closing documents and also ensure that the process goes as smoothly as possible by exerting good due diligence. Due to the large amount of capital usually involved and the varying sources of capital for investment, an independent third-party escrow account is used for the transaction process. While commercial real estate closing is typically longer than residential, there are more means of resolving disagreements in commercial real estate than residential. Always consult with your attorney through the whole process of purchase, from sending offers to closing the deal.
